q-russland-osteuropa-09#explanation: Without a yarlyk from the Golden Horde no Russian prince could rule; the princes of Moscow were especially skilful at obtaining it.
q-russland-osteuropa-10#question: Whom did Alexander Nevsky fight on frozen Lake Peipus in 1242?
q-russland-osteuropa-10#explanation: Alexander defeated an army of the Livonian Order, a branch of the Teutonic Order; he had already beaten the Swedes on the Neva in 1240.
q-russland-osteuropa-11#question: What was the name of the popular assembly that elected mayors and summoned princes in Novgorod?
q-russland-osteuropa-11#explanation: The veche made Novgorod a city republic until Ivan III had its bell taken to Moscow in 1478.
q-russland-osteuropa-12#question: On what did people in Novgorod write the everyday letters that archaeologists have been finding in the ground since 1951?
q-russland-osteuropa-12#explanation: More than a thousand birch-bark documents show that merchants, craftsmen and women in Novgorod could also read and write.
q-russland-osteuropa-13#question: Which prince of Moscow bore the byname Kalita, "Moneybag"?
q-russland-osteuropa-13#explanation: Ivan I collected tribute for the Horde, bought up land and brought the metropolitan to Moscow.
q-russland-osteuropa-14#question: Which grand prince defeated an army of the Horde on the field of Kulikovo in 1380?
q-russland-osteuropa-14#explanation: After the victory on the Don, Dmitry received the byname Donskoy.
q-russland-osteuropa-15#question: Who led the army of the Horde on the field of Kulikovo in 1380?
q-russland-osteuropa-15#explanation: Mamai then controlled the western part of the Horde; two years later Khan Tokhtamysh devastated Moscow.
q-russland-osteuropa-16#question: What was agreed in the Union of Krewo in 1385?
q-russland-osteuropa-16#choices.0: Poland and Lithuania divided Ukraine along the Dnieper
q-russland-osteuropa-16#choices.1: Moscow would pay no more tribute to the Horde
q-russland-osteuropa-16#choices.2: Lithuania ceded Samogitia to the Teutonic Order
q-russland-osteuropa-16#choices.3: Jogaila was to be baptized and marry Queen Jadwiga of Poland
q-russland-osteuropa-16#explanation: The union joined Poland and Lithuania in a personal union and began the Christianization of Lithuania.
q-russland-osteuropa-17#question: Who defeated the Teutonic Order at the Battle of Grunwald (Tannenberg) in 1410?
q-russland-osteuropa-17#choices.0: An army of Moscow and Novgorod
q-russland-osteuropa-17#choices.1: An army of Poland and Lithuania
q-russland-osteuropa-17#choices.2: An army of Sweden and Denmark
q-russland-osteuropa-17#choices.3: An army of the Golden Horde
q-russland-osteuropa-17#explanation: King Władysław II Jagiełło and Grand Duke Vytautas won; Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen fell.
q-russland-osteuropa-18#question: What happened at the Great Stand on the Ugra in 1480?
q-russland-osteuropa-18#choices.0: Ivan IV captured the city of Kazan after a long siege
q-russland-osteuropa-18#choices.1: Lithuania and Poland merged into a common state
q-russland-osteuropa-18#choices.2: The Mongols defeated an army of the Russian princes for the first time
q-russland-osteuropa-18#choices.3: After weeks of facing each other the khan withdrew, and Moscow stopped paying tribute
q-russland-osteuropa-18#explanation: Without a major battle, Moscow's dependence on the Horde ended; later historians placed the end of the "Tatar yoke" here.
q-russland-osteuropa-19#question: Which niece of the last Byzantine emperor did Ivan III marry in 1472?
q-russland-osteuropa-19#explanation: The marriage underlined Moscow's claim to the legacy of Byzantium; the double-headed eagle also came into use under Ivan III.
q-russland-osteuropa-20#question: Which city republic had to submit to Ivan III for good in 1478?
q-russland-osteuropa-20#explanation: Ivan III had Novgorod's veche bell taken to Moscow and resettled many boyar families.
q-russland-osteuropa-21#question: In which year was Ivan IV crowned tsar?
q-russland-osteuropa-21#explanation: On 16 January 1547 Metropolitan Makary crowned him in the Kremlin as the first Russian ruler to bear the title of tsar.
q-russland-osteuropa-22#question: Which khanate on the Volga did Ivan IV conquer in 1552?
q-russland-osteuropa-22#explanation: With Kazan and, four years later, Astrakhan, Moscow controlled the whole of the Volga.
q-russland-osteuropa-23#question: Which building on Red Square commemorates the conquest of Kazan?
q-russland-osteuropa-23#explanation: The colourful St Basil's Cathedral was built from 1555 to 1561 as a church of thanksgiving for the victory.
q-russland-osteuropa-24#choices.0: An assembly of the land that elected the new tsar in 1613
q-russland-osteuropa-24#choices.1: A special domain of Ivan IV from which his bodyguard persecuted supposed traitors
q-russland-osteuropa-24#choices.2: The self-government of peasants in the villages of the tsarist empire
q-russland-osteuropa-24#choices.3: The seat of the Zaporozhian Cossacks on an island in the Dnieper
q-russland-osteuropa-24#explanation: From 1565 to 1572 the oprichniki terrorized boyars, clergy and entire towns.
q-russland-osteuropa-25#question: Which city did Ivan IV have the oprichniki devastate at the beginning of 1570?
q-russland-osteuropa-25#explanation: Ivan suspected Novgorod of treason; thousands of inhabitants were killed, exact figures are unknown.
q-russland-osteuropa-26#question: With the death of which tsar did the Muscovite line of the Rurikids die out in 1598?
q-russland-osteuropa-26#explanation: After the death of the childless Fyodor I, the Time of Troubles began.
q-russland-osteuropa-27#question: Who led the popular militia that drove the Polish-Lithuanian occupiers out of Moscow in 1612?
q-russland-osteuropa-27#choices.2: Kuzma Minin and Prince Dmitry Pozharsky
q-russland-osteuropa-27#explanation: The merchant Minin from Nizhny Novgorod and Prince Pozharsky liberated the Kremlin in the autumn of 1612.
q-russland-osteuropa-28#question: Which assembly elected Michael Romanov tsar in 1613?
q-russland-osteuropa-28#explanation: The Zemsky Sobor was an assembly of the land made up of representatives of the nobility, clergy, towns and Cossacks.
q-russland-osteuropa-29#question: Which state was created by the Union of Lublin in 1569?
q-russland-osteuropa-29#choices.0: The Commonwealth of the Two Nations (Poland-Lithuania)
q-russland-osteuropa-29#explanation: Poland and Lithuania received a common king and parliament but kept their own offices and laws.
q-russland-osteuropa-30#question: What did the liberum veto mean in the Polish-Lithuanian parliament?
q-russland-osteuropa-30#choices.0: The king could reject any law without giving reasons
q-russland-osteuropa-30#choices.1: Peasants could sue their landlord in court
q-russland-osteuropa-30#choices.2: A single deputy could block decisions by objecting
q-russland-osteuropa-30#choices.3: Every noble could freely choose his denomination
q-russland-osteuropa-30#explanation: The principle of unanimity paralysed the Commonwealth in the 17th and 18th centuries until the constitution of 1791 abolished it.
q-russland-osteuropa-31#question: What came into being through the Union of Brest in 1596?
q-russland-osteuropa-31#choices.0: An alliance between Poland-Lithuania and Sweden against Moscow
q-russland-osteuropa-31#choices.1: The Greek Catholic Church, which recognized the pope and kept the Eastern rite
q-russland-osteuropa-31#choices.2: The first university in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania
q-russland-osteuropa-31#choices.3: A peace treaty between the Cossacks and the Crimean Tatars
q-russland-osteuropa-31#explanation: Some of the Orthodox bishops in Poland-Lithuania placed themselves under Rome; their church remains widespread especially in western Ukraine.
q-russland-osteuropa-32#question: In which city did Francysk Skaryna of Polotsk print his Psalter in 1517?
q-russland-osteuropa-32#explanation: From 1517 to 1519 Skaryna printed biblical books in an East Slavic literary language in Prague, and later worked in Vilnius.
q-russland-osteuropa-33#question: Who led the great Cossack uprising against Poland-Lithuania in 1648?
q-russland-osteuropa-33#explanation: After his first victories Khmelnytsky established a Hetmanate in Ukraine.
q-russland-osteuropa-34#question: In which place did Khmelnytsky place himself under the tsar in 1654?
q-russland-osteuropa-34#explanation: Ukrainian and Russian historians still interpret the Pereiaslav agreement differently.
q-russland-osteuropa-35#question: What was the fortified centre of the Zaporozhian Cossacks on the lower Dnieper called?
q-russland-osteuropa-35#explanation: The Zaporozhian Sich lay beyond the rapids of the Dnieper, hence the name "Zaporozhian", meaning "beyond the rapids".
q-russland-osteuropa-36#question: Which patriarch's church reforms triggered the Russian church schism in the 17th century?
q-russland-osteuropa-36#explanation: Nikon had books and rites changed to follow Greek models; the council of 1666/67 confirmed the reforms.
q-russland-osteuropa-37#question: What are the believers who rejected the church reforms of the 17th century called?
q-russland-osteuropa-37#explanation: The Old Believers held on to the old rites, such as crossing themselves with two fingers, and were persecuted for a long time.
q-russland-osteuropa-38#question: Near which town in present-day Ukraine did Peter the Great defeat the army of Charles XII in 1709?
q-russland-osteuropa-38#explanation: The victory at Poltava ended Sweden's supremacy in the north and made Russia a great power.
q-russland-osteuropa-39#question: Which Cossack hetman went over to Charles XII during the Great Northern War?
q-russland-osteuropa-39#explanation: Mazepa hoped Sweden would secure the independence of the Hetmanate and, after Poltava, fled with Charles to the Ottoman Empire.
q-russland-osteuropa-40#question: What did the Polish-Lithuanian parliament adopt on 3 May 1791?
q-russland-osteuropa-40#choices.0: The cession of Lithuania to Russia
q-russland-osteuropa-40#choices.1: A constitution that abolished the liberum veto
q-russland-osteuropa-40#choices.2: The election of a Russian grand duke as king
q-russland-osteuropa-40#choices.3: The dissolution of the union with Lithuania
q-russland-osteuropa-40#explanation: The Constitution of 3 May is regarded as the first modern written constitution in Europe; the day is a Polish national holiday.
q-russland-osteuropa-41#question: Who led the uprising against Russia and Prussia in 1794?
q-russland-osteuropa-41#explanation: Kościuszko won at Racławice but was captured at Maciejowice in October 1794.
q-russland-osteuropa-42#question: In which year did Poland-Lithuania vanish from the map with the third partition?
q-russland-osteuropa-42#explanation: In 1795 Russia, Prussia and Austria divided the remaining territory among themselves.
q-russland-osteuropa-43#question: Which navigator in Russian service reached the coast of Alaska in 1741?
q-russland-osteuropa-43#explanation: The Dane Vitus Bering led the Great Northern Expedition; he died in 1741 on the island later named after him.
q-russland-osteuropa-44#question: To which country did Russia sell Alaska in 1867?
q-russland-osteuropa-44#explanation: The United States paid 7.2 million dollars; Canada only became a self-governing dominion that same year.
q-russland-osteuropa-45#question: Where does the name of the Decembrists come from?
q-russland-osteuropa-45#choices.2: From the tsar's decree that exiled them
q-russland-osteuropa-45#choices.3: From the decade they had to spend in exile
q-russland-osteuropa-45#explanation: The Russian word for December is "dekabr"; the revolt took place on 14 December 1825.
q-russland-osteuropa-46#question: Which tsar abolished serfdom in Russia in 1861?
q-russland-osteuropa-46#explanation: With the manifesto of 19 February 1861 by the Julian calendar, some 23 million privately owned serfs were freed.
q-russland-osteuropa-47#question: What were the zemstvos introduced in the tsarist empire in 1864?
q-russland-osteuropa-47#choices.0: Military colonies on the border with the steppe
q-russland-osteuropa-47#choices.3: Secret police authorities of the tsar
q-russland-osteuropa-47#explanation: The zemstvos looked after schools, health care and roads in the countryside; nobles, townspeople and peasants were represented in them.
q-russland-osteuropa-48#question: Which collection of poems by Taras Shevchenko became the cornerstone of modern Ukrainian literature in 1840?
q-russland-osteuropa-48#explanation: "Kobzar" celebrated the history of the Cossacks and the suffering of the peasants in the Ukrainian language.
q-russland-osteuropa-49#question: What did the Ems Ukaz of 1876 prohibit?
q-russland-osteuropa-49#choices.0: The emigration of peasants to Siberia
q-russland-osteuropa-49#choices.1: The printing and import of most books in the Ukrainian language
q-russland-osteuropa-49#choices.2: The use of the Polish language in church
q-russland-osteuropa-49#choices.3: The founding of trade unions in factories
q-russland-osteuropa-49#explanation: Ukrainian authors then moved their work to Galicia under Austrian rule.
q-russland-osteuropa-50#question: Which event in January 1905 triggered the first Russian revolution?
q-russland-osteuropa-50#choices.1: The mutiny on the battleship Potemkin
q-russland-osteuropa-50#choices.2: The fall of the fortress of Sevastopol
q-russland-osteuropa-50#explanation: Soldiers fired on a peaceful procession of workers who wanted to deliver a petition to the tsar.
q-russland-osteuropa-51#question: What did Nicholas II promise in the October Manifesto of 1905?
q-russland-osteuropa-51#choices.0: Civil rights and an elected Duma
q-russland-osteuropa-51#choices.2: The return of the partitioned lands to Poland
q-russland-osteuropa-51#choices.3: An immediate end to the war against Germany
q-russland-osteuropa-51#explanation: The Duma, however, had limited powers, and the tsar soon dissolved the first two.
q-russland-osteuropa-52#question: Which tsar abdicated after the February Revolution of 1917?
q-russland-osteuropa-52#explanation: With the abdication of Nicholas II in March 1917, the rule of the Romanovs ended after more than 300 years.
q-suedostasien-01#question: In which present-day country is the Buddhist temple mountain of Borobudur located?
q-suedostasien-01#explanation: Borobudur lies in Central Java, Indonesia, and was built around 780 to 830 under the Shailendra dynasty.
q-suedostasien-02#question: In which river delta was Óc Eo, the port of the kingdom of Funan, located?
q-suedostasien-02#explanation: Óc Eo lay in the Mekong Delta in present-day southern Vietnam; finds there come from India, China and even the Roman Empire.
q-suedostasien-03#question: To which religion was Borobudur dedicated?
q-suedostasien-03#explanation: Borobudur is a Mahayana Buddhist sanctuary; its reliefs show the life of the Buddha and the path to enlightenment.
q-suedostasien-04#question: Which strait did the kingdom of Srivijaya control from Sumatra?
q-suedostasien-04#explanation: From Palembang Srivijaya dominated the Strait of Malacca and the Sunda Strait, through which sea trade between India and China passed.
q-suedostasien-05#question: Which king was consecrated as universal monarch on Phnom Kulen in 802 and founded the Khmer Empire?
q-suedostasien-05#explanation: In 802 Jayavarman II declared the independence of the Khmer and laid the foundation of the empire of Angkor.
q-suedostasien-06#question: In which year did Ngô Quyền defeat the Chinese fleet on the Bạch Đằng River?
q-suedostasien-06#explanation: The victory of 938 ended roughly a thousand years of Chinese rule over present-day northern Vietnam.
q-suedostasien-07#question: What stratagem did Ngô Quyền use to win the battle on the Bạch Đằng?
q-suedostasien-07#choices.0: He dammed the river so the fleet ran aground
q-suedostasien-07#choices.1: He sent burning rafts against the ships
q-suedostasien-07#choices.2: He had a bridge over the river collapse
q-suedostasien-07#choices.3: He had iron-tipped stakes driven into the riverbed, which impaled the ships at low tide
q-suedostasien-07#explanation: Ngô Quyền lured the fleet over the hidden stakes at high tide; when the water fell, the ships were stuck and destroyed.
q-suedostasien-08#question: Which capital, with the Bayon at its centre, did Jayavarman VII build?
q-suedostasien-08#explanation: After 1181 Jayavarman VII built the walled city of Angkor Thom, at whose centre stands the Bayon.
q-suedostasien-09#question: What are the towers of the Bayon at Angkor famous for?
q-suedostasien-09#explanation: The many towers of the Bayon bear large stone faces looking out in all directions.
q-suedostasien-10#question: Which religion did Jayavarman VII particularly promote?
q-suedostasien-10#explanation: Jayavarman VII was a Mahayana Buddhist and dedicated many of his buildings to the Buddha and bodhisattvas.
q-suedostasien-11#question: Which king made Pagan the centre of a great kingdom in Burma from 1044?
q-suedostasien-11#explanation: Anawrahta reigned from 1044 and united large parts of the Irrawaddy valley under Pagan's rule.
q-suedostasien-12#question: To which god is the tallest temple of Prambanan on Java dedicated?
q-suedostasien-12#explanation: The main temple of Prambanan, consecrated in 856, is dedicated to Shiva; beside it stand temples to Vishnu and Brahma.
q-suedostasien-13#question: Which king of Sukhothai is associated with the creation of the Thai script?
q-suedostasien-13#explanation: An inscription of 1292 attributes the Thai script to Ramkhamhaeng, although its authenticity is disputed.
q-suedostasien-14#question: Why is the Ramkhamhaeng inscription of 1292 disputed among scholars?
q-suedostasien-14#choices.0: Because it is written in Chinese
q-suedostasien-14#choices.1: Because some scholars doubt that it really dates from the 13th century
q-suedostasien-14#choices.2: Because it was lost in the Second World War
q-suedostasien-14#choices.3: Because it was found in Burma
q-suedostasien-14#explanation: The inscription was found in 1833 by the future King Mongkut; since the 1980s some scholars have considered it to be later.
q-suedostasien-15#question: From which empire did Sukhothai break free around 1238?
q-suedostasien-15#explanation: Around 1238 Thai chiefs drove the Khmer governor out of Sukhothai.
q-suedostasien-16#question: Who founded the kingdom of Majapahit on Java in 1293?
q-suedostasien-16#explanation: With the help of a Mongol fleet Raden Wijaya defeated his rival and then founded Majapahit.
q-suedostasien-17#question: Which foreign fleet unintentionally helped Raden Wijaya found Majapahit in 1293?
q-suedostasien-17#choices.1: A fleet of the Mongol Yuan dynasty
q-suedostasien-17#choices.2: A fleet of the Chola Empire
q-suedostasien-17#explanation: Kublai Khan had sent a punitive expedition to Java; Raden Wijaya used it against his rival and then drove the Mongols out.
q-suedostasien-18#question: According to Javanese tradition, who swore the Palapa oath to unite the archipelago under Majapahit?
q-suedostasien-18#explanation: The minister Gajah Mada is said to have sworn to renounce pleasures until the archipelago was united under Majapahit.
q-suedostasien-19#question: Which work of 1365 describes the court and extent of Majapahit?
q-suedostasien-19#explanation: The eulogy Nagarakretagama by the poet Prapanca describes the court of Hayam Wuruk and lists dependent territories.
q-suedostasien-20#question: Where did Sultan Malik al-Salih rule, whose gravestone of 1297 is regarded as early evidence of Islam in Southeast Asia?
q-suedostasien-20#explanation: Malik al-Salih ruled Samudera Pasai in northern Sumatra, one of the first Islamic sultanates in the region.
q-suedostasien-21#question: How did Islam mainly spread in Southeast Asia?
q-suedostasien-21#choices.1: Through forced conversions by the Ottomans
q-suedostasien-21#choices.2: Through merchants, scholars and Sufis along the trade routes
q-suedostasien-21#explanation: Islam arrived in the ports with Muslim traders and scholars and was adopted from there by rulers and their peoples.
q-suedostasien-22#question: Which prince from Palembang founded Malacca around 1400?
q-suedostasien-22#explanation: Parameswara fled from Sumatra via Temasek and founded Malacca on the west coast of the Malay Peninsula around 1400.
q-suedostasien-23#question: In which year did the Portuguese conquer Malacca?
q-suedostasien-23#explanation: Afonso de Albuquerque took Malacca in August 1511, opening the European colonial era in Southeast Asia.
q-suedostasien-24#question: Who led the Portuguese in the conquest of Malacca in 1511?
q-suedostasien-24#explanation: Afonso de Albuquerque, governor of Portuguese India, conquered Malacca from his base at Goa.
q-suedostasien-25#question: Which spices made the Moluccas and the Banda Islands so coveted by Europeans?
q-suedostasien-25#explanation: For a long time cloves grew only in the northern Moluccas and nutmeg only on the Banda Islands.
q-suedostasien-26#question: Who founded Manila in 1571 as the capital of the Spanish Philippines?
q-suedostasien-26#explanation: In 1571 Legazpi captured the settlement of Maynila and made it the capital of the colony.
q-suedostasien-27#question: Who are the Philippines named after?
q-suedostasien-27#explanation: In 1543 a Spanish expedition named the islands after the heir to the throne, Philip, later King Philip II.
q-suedostasien-28#question: Which Chinese monk reported more than a thousand Buddhist monks in Srivijaya in the 7th century?
q-suedostasien-28#explanation: Yijing stayed in Srivijaya on his journey to India and advised pilgrims to learn Sanskrit there.
q-suedostasien-29#question: Which city did the Dutch East India Company found on Java in 1619?
q-suedostasien-29#explanation: Jan Pieterszoon Coen founded Batavia on the site of the destroyed Jayakarta as the VOC's headquarters.
q-suedostasien-30#question: Which present-day capital grew out of Dutch Batavia?
q-suedostasien-30#explanation: Batavia is today's Jakarta, the capital of Indonesia.
q-suedostasien-31#question: Besides founding Batavia, what is Jan Pieterszoon Coen notorious for?
q-suedostasien-31#choices.1: A war against the Spanish in Manila
q-suedostasien-31#choices.2: The conquest of the Banda Islands, in which much of the population was killed, enslaved or driven out
q-suedostasien-31#choices.3: Driving the English out of India
q-suedostasien-31#explanation: To enforce the nutmeg monopoly, Coen had the Banda Islands conquered in 1621 and their population largely wiped out.
q-suedostasien-32#question: In which year was the Dutch East India Company (VOC) founded?
q-suedostasien-32#explanation: The VOC was formed in 1602 as a merger of several trading companies and received the Dutch monopoly on trade with Asia.
q-suedostasien-33#question: Who captured and destroyed the Siamese capital Ayutthaya in 1767?
q-suedostasien-33#explanation: Konbaung troops under King Hsinbyushin took Ayutthaya in April 1767 and burned the city.
q-suedostasien-34#question: Which city did Rama I make the new capital of Siam in 1782?
q-suedostasien-34#explanation: In 1782 Rama I founded the Chakri dynasty and moved the capital to Bangkok.
q-suedostasien-35#question: Who founded the Burmese Konbaung dynasty in 1752?
q-suedostasien-35#explanation: Alaungpaya reunited Burma and founded the Konbaung dynasty, which ruled until 1885.
q-suedostasien-36#question: Who united Vietnam in 1802 and founded the Nguyễn dynasty?
q-suedostasien-36#explanation: Nguyễn Ánh defeated the Tây Sơn, took the imperial name Gia Long in 1802 and ruled all of Vietnam.
q-suedostasien-37#question: Which city was the capital of the Nguyễn emperors?
q-suedostasien-37#explanation: Gia Long made Huế in central Vietnam his capital and had a large citadel built there.
q-suedostasien-38#question: Which uprising from 1771 overthrew Vietnam's old ruling houses and preceded the Nguyễn dynasty?
q-suedostasien-38#explanation: The Tây Sơn brothers overthrew the Nguyễn and Trịnh lords before Nguyễn Ánh defeated them.
q-suedostasien-39#question: Who founded Singapore as a British free port in 1819?
q-suedostasien-39#explanation: Stamford Raffles acquired the island in 1819 through a treaty with a prince of Johor.
q-suedostasien-40#question: Which three ports did the British combine into the Straits Settlements in 1826?
q-suedostasien-40#explanation: Penang, Malacca and Singapore formed the Straits Settlements on the Strait of Malacca.
q-suedostasien-41#question: In which year did British troops take Mandalay and end the Burmese monarchy?
q-suedostasien-41#explanation: In the Third Anglo-Burmese War of 1885 King Thibaw was deposed; at the start of 1886 Burma became part of British India.
q-suedostasien-42#question: Which treaty of 1824 divided the British and Dutch spheres of interest along the Strait of Malacca?
q-suedostasien-42#explanation: Under the Treaty of London of 1824 the British received the Malay Peninsula and the Dutch the islands south of the strait.
q-suedostasien-43#question: In which year did France combine its possessions into the Indochinese Union?
q-suedostasien-43#explanation: French Indochina was created in 1887 from Cochinchina, Annam, Tonkin and Cambodia; Laos was added in 1893.
q-suedostasien-44#question: Which people founded the kingdom of Champa on the coast of present-day central Vietnam?
q-suedostasien-44#explanation: The Cham spoke an Austronesian language and built numerous Hindu temples at Mỹ Sơn.
q-suedostasien-45#question: Which king of Siam modernized administration, schools and the army from 1868 and gradually abolished slavery?
q-suedostasien-45#explanation: Chulalongkorn (Rama V) reigned from 1868 to 1910 and is regarded as Siam's great reformer.
q-suedostasien-46#question: What role did Siam play between British Burma and French Indochina?
q-suedostasien-46#choices.0: It was partitioned between the two powers
q-suedostasien-46#choices.2: It remained independent and served as a buffer state
q-suedostasien-46#choices.3: It became part of French Indochina
q-suedostasien-46#explanation: Siam remained the only independent state in Southeast Asia, but had to cede outlying territories to both powers.
q-suedostasien-47#question: Which territories did Siam have to cede to France after the Paknam crisis of 1893?
q-suedostasien-47#choices.1: The territories east of the Mekong, today's Laos
q-suedostasien-47#explanation: After French gunboats had sailed up to Bangkok, Siam ceded the territories east of the Mekong.
q-suedostasien-48#question: Which secret society began the uprising against Spanish rule in the Philippines in 1896?
q-suedostasien-48#explanation: The Katipunan, founded in 1892 by Andrés Bonifacio, aimed to win independence by force of arms.
q-suedostasien-49#question: Which writer was shot by the Spanish in Manila on 30 December 1896?
q-suedostasien-49#explanation: José Rizal, author of Noli Me Tángere, was executed despite having advocated peaceful reform.
q-suedostasien-50#question: Who proclaimed the independence of the Philippines on 12 June 1898?
q-suedostasien-50#explanation: Emilio Aguinaldo proclaimed independence at Kawit and in 1899 became president of the First Philippine Republic.
q-suedostasien-51#question: To which country did Spain cede the Philippines in the Treaty of Paris of 1898?
q-suedostasien-51#explanation: After the Spanish-American War the Philippines passed to the USA, against which the Filipinos fought from 1899.
q-suedostasien-52#question: What did the Dutch Cultivation System require of Java's peasants from 1830?
q-suedostasien-52#choices.2: To serve in the colonial army
q-suedostasien-52#choices.3: To devote part of their land or labour to export crops such as coffee and sugar
q-suedostasien-52#explanation: Villages had to grow export crops that the state bought cheaply; this brought the Netherlands large profits and Java famines.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-01#question: Which monastery off the coast of Northumbria did Vikings raid in 793?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-01#explanation: The raid on Lindisfarne on 8 June 793 is regarded as the beginning of the Viking Age.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-02#question: Which city did Vikings sack at Easter 845 before Charles the Bald bought their departure with silver?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-02#explanation: A fleet sailed up the Seine and left only after being paid 7,000 pounds of silver.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-03#question: Which Viking leader received the land around Rouen in 911, which became Normandy?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-03#explanation: Rollo came to terms with Charles the Simple and founded Norman rule on the lower Seine.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-04#question: What was the name of the assembly that first met in Iceland around 930?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-04#explanation: The Althing met every summer at Þingvellir and made laws for all of Iceland.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-05#question: Who led the first Norse settlers to Greenland around 985?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-05#explanation: Erik the Red used his banishment from Iceland to explore Greenland and then returned with settlers.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-06#question: Which seafarer reached the land in North America that the sagas call “Vinland” around 1000?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-06#explanation: Leif Eriksson, the son of Erik the Red, sailed west from Greenland and spent the winter in Vinland.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-07#question: Where in Newfoundland were the remains of a Norse settlement from around 1000 found?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-07#explanation: Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad discovered the site in 1960; it is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-08#question: Which Danish king boasted on the Jelling runestone that he had made the Danes Christian?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-08#explanation: Harald Bluetooth had the great Jelling stone erected in honour of his parents Gorm and Thyra.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-09#question: Which king ruled England, Denmark and Norway at the same time around 1028?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-09#explanation: Cnut the Great became king of England in 1016, inherited Denmark and won Norway in 1028.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-10#question: In which battle did the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada fall in 1066?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-10#explanation: Harald Hardrada was defeated by the English king Harold Godwinson at Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-11#question: Which queen united Denmark, Norway and Sweden in the Kalmar Union in 1397?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-11#explanation: Margaret I had her great-nephew Eric of Pomerania crowned at Kalmar and herself ruled until 1412.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-12#question: Which type of ship was the typical warship of the Vikings?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-12#explanation: The slender longship with sail and oars was seaworthy and could penetrate far up rivers.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-13#question: What are the characters called that Scandinavians carved into stones in the Viking Age?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-13#explanation: The younger runic row of the Viking Age had 16 characters; thousands of runestones survive.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-14#question: Which god was, in Norse mythology, the lord of the gods and the god of wisdom and poetry?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-14#explanation: Odin was regarded as the father of the gods; Thor was the thunder god and Freyr a god of fertility.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-15#question: What was the Scandinavian-settled area in eastern England, where Danish law applied, called?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-15#explanation: After Alfred’s victory at Edington in 878 a boundary arose; the area to the north and east of it was later called the Danelaw.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-16#question: Which Anglo-Saxon king was the only one to hold out against the Great Heathen Army?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-16#explanation: Alfred the Great of Wessex defeated the Vikings at Edington in 878.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-17#question: Which Icelandic scholar wrote the Prose Edda around 1220?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-17#explanation: Snorri Sturluson wrote the Prose Edda as a handbook of poetry and later Heimskringla.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-18#question: Which town did Norwegian Vikings found as a fortified camp in Ireland in 841?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-18#explanation: The longphort on the Liffey developed into a Scandinavian-ruled trading town.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-19#question: Which year is usually taken as the end of the Viking Age?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-19#explanation: With the death of Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge in 1066 the great Viking expeditions ended.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-20#question: What were the Scandinavian traders and warriors called who travelled along the Russian rivers to Byzantium?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-20#explanation: In the East they were called Varangians or Rus; some later served in the Byzantine emperor’s bodyguard.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-21#question: In which year did the Great Heathen Army land in East Anglia?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-21#explanation: The army came ashore in 865, took York in 866 and conquered several kingdoms in the following years.
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-22#question: Which city did the Great Heathen Army capture in 866?
q-wikinger-nordeuropa-22#explanation: York, Anglo-Saxon Eoforwic, became the centre of Scandinavian rule in northern England under the name Jórvík.
